prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Large-scale image-to-video diffusion models have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generating dynamic motion from a single conditioning image. However, these models typically operate in a unilateral manner—predicting the future from a present frame. They lack the native ability to perform "keyframe interpolation," or generating a coherent video sequence that connects a specific start frame to a specific end frame.

Current solutions to this problem are suboptimal. Training a dedicated interpolation model from scratch requires prohibitive computational resources and data. Alternatively, naive approaches that attempt to merge independent forward (from start) and backward (from end) generations often fail to produce continuous motion. These methods frequently result in temporal incoherence, where objects oscillate—moving forward and then reversing—rather than progressing smoothly from the start to the target state. We need a method to adapt existing pre-trained models for bounded, two-frame generation without massive retraining.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the temporal motion priors within a pre-trained image-to-video model are reversible. Specifically, we hypothesize that the **temporal self-attention maps** generated during a forward prediction pass encode the essential trajectory of motion. By geometrically rotating these attention maps (reversing the temporal interactions), we can provide a strong structural guide for generating the sequence in reverse.

We believe that by synchronizing a forward generation process and a backward generation process via these shared, rotated attention maps, we can enforce "forward-backward motion consistency." This will ensure that the motion generated from the start frame and the motion generated from the end frame are not just plausible individually, but are mathematically forced to be the inverse of one another, resulting in a seamless meeting in the middle.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to adapt a pre-trained image-to-video diffusion model into a bidirectional interpolator using a two-stage strategy:

**1. Lightweight Backward Adaptation via Attention Rotation**
We will create a specific "backward-predicting" version of the base model. However, rather than retraining the U-Net from scratch, we will employ a lightweight fine-tuning strategy.
*   **Input Strategy:** This model will take the *end* frame as input to predict the past. Crucially, it will also accept the **rotated temporal self-attention maps** extracted from the pre-trained forward model.
*   **Parameter Efficient Tuning:** We will freeze the vast majority of the model parameters. We will only optimize the value and output projection matrices within the temporal attention layers. This allows the model to learn how to interpret the inverted attention maps to synthesize backward motion that mirrors the forward statistics.

**2. Dual-Directional Sampling with Fusion**
During the inference phase, we will employ a joint sampling process that harmonizes the two directions:
*   **Parallel Denoising:** We will run two simultaneous diffusion processes: one predicting forward from the start frame (using the frozen base model) and one predicting backward from the end frame (using our fine-tuned adapter).
*   **Attention Synchronization:** The backward process will not compute its own attention structure independently. Instead, it will use the 180-degree rotated attention maps extracted dynamically from the forward process. This locks the two trajectories together.
*   **Noise Fusion:** At each sampling step, we will combine the noise predictions from the forward pass and the (temporally flipped) backward pass. This fused estimate will guide the next step of the denoising, ensuring the generated content remains consistent with both boundary frames throughout the generation.

## Expected Contribution
We expect to deliver a method that enables high-quality keyframe interpolation using existing large-scale diffusion models with minimal additional training cost. Theoretically, this will demonstrate that temporal self-attention maps in diffusion models possess a reversible geometric property that can be exploited for control. Practically, this approach will allow for the generation of smooth, long-term motion between distant keyframes, overcoming the "oscillation" artifacts common in naive bidirectional sampling and surpassing the limitations of traditional optical flow-based interpolation.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed an experiment to adapt a pre-trained large-scale image-to-video diffusion model (Stable Video Diffusion - SVD) for the task of keyframe interpolation. The core technical approach involved a lightweight fine-tuning technique to predict backward motion and a dual-directional sampling process.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Davis Dataset:** 117 input pairs created from 1080p videos. Features subject articulated motions (animal or human motions).
    *   **Pexels Dataset:** 106 input pairs collected from high-resolution (1080p) videos from Pexels. Features directional dynamic scene motions (vehicles moving, people running, surfing, wave movements, time-lapse).
    *   **Conditioning:** All input pairs were at least 25 frames apart ($\geq$ 1 second) and had corresponding ground truth video clips.
    *   **Training Data:** 100 high-quality synthetic videos generated by SVD, selected for large object motion (animal running, vehicle moving, people walking).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **FID (Fréchet Inception Distance):** Measures the distance between distributions of generated frames and actual frames. Lower is better.
    *   **FVD (Fréchet Video Distance):** Measures the distance between distributions of generated videos and actual videos. Lower is better.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **FILM:** A flow-based frame interpolation method (state-of-the-art for large motion).
    *   **TRF:** A method adapting SVD for bounded video generation using forward and reversed-forward fusion.
    *   **DynamiCrafter:** A large-scale image-to-video model with a specific keyframe interpolation feature (note: generates at $512 \times 320$ resolution, compared to our $1024 \times 576$).
    *   **Ablation Variants:**
        *   *Ours w/o RA:* Fine-tuning all parameters ($W_{q, k, v, o}$) without rotated attention maps.
        *   *Ours w/o FT:* Using rotated attention maps in "up" blocks only, without fine-tuning any parameters.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Base Model:** Stable Video Diffusion (SVD).
    *   **Fine-tuning Scope:** Only the value ($W_v$) and output ($W_o$) projection matrices in the temporal self-attention layers were fine-tuned (less than 2% of U-Net parameters).
    *   **Hardware:** 4 A100 GPUs.
    *   **Optimizer:** Adam ($lr = 1e-4$, $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, weight decay $= 1e-2$).
    *   **Training Volume:** Approximately $15,000$ iterations with a batch size of 4.
    *   **Sampling:** 50 sampling steps using the EDM sampler.
    *   **SVD Hyperparameters:** Default motion bucket id = 127 (unless otherwise noted in ablations), noise augmentation strength = 0.02.
    *   **Resolution:** Generated videos at $1024 \times 576$.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Quantitative Comparison with Baselines and Ablation Variants**
*Performance comparison on Pexels and Davis datasets. "Ours" represents the full proposed method.*

| Method | Pexels FID $\downarrow$ | Pexels FVD $\downarrow$ | Davis FID $\downarrow$ | Davis FVD $\downarrow$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| FILM | 25.16 | 371.83 | 41.85 | 1048.65 |
| TRF | 31.43 | 563.16 | 36.79 | 563.07 |
| DynamiCrafter | 32.06 | 393.12 | 38.32 | 439.74 |
| Ours w/o RA | 26.42 | 458.76 | 36.70 | 549.98 |
| Ours w/o FT | 37.68 | 555.10 | 47.23 | 604.76 |
| **Ours** | **22.99** | **306.84** | **32.68** | **424.69** |

**Table 2: Ablation Study on Motion Bucket ID**
*Impact of the SVD conditioning parameter `motion_bucket_id` on model performance.*

| Method (Configuration) | Pexels FID $\downarrow$ | Pexels FVD $\downarrow$ | Davis FID $\downarrow$ | Davis FVD $\downarrow$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| FILM | 25.16 | 371.83 | 41.85 | 1048.65 |
| TRF | 31.43 | 563.16 | 36.79 | 563.07 |
| Ours (motion bucket id = 255) | 22.18 | 306.61 | 34.06 | 426.53 |
| Ours (motion bucket id = 65) | 23.33 | 270.27 | 32.75 | 491.85 |
| Ours (motion bucket id = 127) | 22.99 | 306.84 | 32.68 | 424.69 |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Comparison with Baselines:**
*   **Observation regarding TRF:** This baseline exhibited back-and-forth motion artifacts. For example, vehicles were observed moving forward and then reversing, or a dog's legs were seen moving backward. This oscillation resulted from fusing a forward video generation with a reversed forward video.
*   **Observation regarding FILM:** This flow-based method struggled with large motions where correspondences were distant. We observed artifacts where objects (e.g., cars) disappeared in the middle frames and reappeared at the end, or where the method simply morphed pixels from the first frame to the last without plausible motion logic. It also tended to produce unambiguous linear motion paths that lacked natural kinematics (e.g., translating a running person without leg articulation).
*   **Observation regarding "Ours":** The proposed method produced motion-consistent videos where the direction of movement (e.g., traffic flow, waves) remained consistent throughout the sequence, effectively bridging distant keyframes.

**Ablation Analysis:**
*   **Effect of Rotated Attention (RA):** When fine-tuning all parameters without the 180-degree rotated temporal attention map, the model failed to guarantee that the backward motion mirrored the forward motion. This led to discrepancies between the two motion paths, resulting in visible blending artifacts in the fused output.
*   **Effect of Fine-Tuning (FT):** When using rotated attention maps without fine-tuning the projection matrices ($W_v, W_o$), the model achieved consistent motion direction but suffered from severe degradation in frame quality (e.g., disfigured human subjects).
*   **Dataset Scale:** Experiments indicated that the method generalizes well even with a small training set (50 videos), with performance improving slowly as the dataset size increased to 150.

**Limitations and Failure Cases:**
*   **Articulated Motion:** While superior to baselines, the method struggled to generate perfectly natural kinematic motions for complex articulated subjects (e.g., running humans/animals). This limitation was traced back to the underlying SVD base model, which failed to generate plausible running kinematics even when conditioned on a single frame.
*   **Sparse Correspondence:** The method failed to fuse motions effectively when the input keyframes had minimal overlapping content (sparse correspondences). For example, in a fast-moving highway scene where only a small portion of cars appeared in both the start and end frames, artifacts appeared in the intermediate frames.
*   **Motion Bucket ID Sensitivity:** On the Pexels dataset, a lower motion bucket ID (65) yielded better FVD scores, while on the Davis dataset, it resulted in worse scores. This suggests sensitivity to the type of motion inherent in the dataset.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.

You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.

The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Recent advancements in large-scale image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models have enabled the generation of high-resolution videos with dynamic motion. However, these models are predominantly designed for uni-directional generation: predicting a future video sequence conditioned on a single starting image. They are ill-equipped for **keyframe interpolation** (generating a coherent video sequence between a specific starting frame $I_0$ and ending frame $I_{N-1}$).

Creating a specialized interpolation model typically requires training from scratch on massive datasets, demanding computational resources unavailable to most research groups. Furthermore, simply adapting existing models by fusing a forward generation (from $I_0$) and a reversed generation (from $I_{N-1}$) using the standard pre-trained weights often fails. This is because real-world motion is asymmetric; a model trained on forward motion cannot simply be reversed to predict backward motion accurately. This naive fusion results in "oscillation" artifacts, where the video progresses forward and then unnaturally reverses direction to meet the end frame, failing to establish a consistent motion path.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can adapt a pre-trained, forward-moving I2V model to perform high-fidelity keyframe interpolation without training from scratch. Our core insight is that the **temporal self-attention maps** within the diffusion U-Net encode the motion structure. By rotating these maps by 180 degrees, we can approximate the structure of backward motion.

We propose a **lightweight fine-tuning mechanism** where we freeze the majority of the pre-trained model and train *only* the value and output projection matrices ($W_v, W_o$) of the temporal attention layers. This fine-tuned "backward model" will accept the rotated attention maps from the frozen "forward model" as a guide. Finally, we propose a **Dual-Directional Diffusion Sampling** process that runs the forward and backward models in parallel, fusing their noise predictions at each step to ensure forward-backward motion consistency.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will build our framework upon Stable Video Diffusion (SVD), a latent diffusion model utilizing a 3D U-Net architecture. Our methodology consists of three distinct components: the mechanism for reversing motion-time association, the lightweight fine-tuning strategy, and the dual-directional sampling algorithm.

### 1. Motion-Time Association via Attention Rotation
The core of motion modeling in the 3D U-Net lies in the temporal self-attention layers. Let the input to such a layer be a spatio-temporal tensor reshaped to $X' \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times N \times C}$, where $N$ is the number of frames. The self-attention mechanism projects this input via matrices $W_q, W_k, W_v$ to obtain Query ($Q$), Key ($K$), and Value ($V$) features. The attention operation is defined as:

$$ \operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}(QK^T / \sqrt{d})V $$

We define the temporal self-attention map as $A = QK^T \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times N \times N}$, which models inter-frame correlations. This map $A$ features the forward motion trajectory.

To generate backward motion, we will explicitly reverse this association. We will derive a rotated attention map set $\{A'_i\}$ by rotating the original forward maps $\{A_i\}$ by 180 degrees (flipping vertically and horizontally). Mathematically, for an attention map $A$, the rotated map $A'$ is defined such that:
$$ A'_{N-j, N-k} = A_{j, k} $$
where $A_{j, k}$ represents the attention score between the $j$-th and $k$-th frames. This ensures that the reverse frame indices maintain the same relative response as the forward video.

### 2. Lightweight Backward Motion Fine-Tuning
We will construct a backward-generation network $f_{\theta'}$ initialized with the pre-trained SVD weights. To ensure efficiency and retain learned motion priors, we will freeze all parameters except for the value projection matrix $W_v$ and the output projection matrix $W_o$ within the temporal self-attention layers.

The training process (Algorithm 1) proceeds as follows:
1.  **Forward Pass (Frozen):** Given a noisy latent $\mathbf{z}_t$, we pass it and the start-frame conditioning $\mathbf{c}_0$ through the pre-trained forward network $f_\theta$. We extract the temporal attention maps $\{A_i\}$.
2.  **Input Preparation:** We reverse the noisy latent video along the time axis, denoted as $\operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{z}_t)$. We compute conditioning $\mathbf{c}_{N-1}$ from the last frame $I_{N-1}$.
3.  **Backward Pass (Trainable):** We feed the reversed latent, $\mathbf{c}_{N-1}$, and the **180-degree rotated attention maps** $\{A'_i\}$ into the backward network $f_{\theta'}$.
4.  **Optimization:** We optimize $\theta'$ (specifically $W_v, W_o$) by minimizing the diffusion loss on the predicted noise. The target vector is the reversed noise of the forward process. The loss function is:
    $$ \mathcal{L}(\theta') = \| f_{\theta'}(\operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{z}_t); t, \mathbf{c}_{N-1}, \{A'_i\}) - \mathbf{y} \|_2^2 $$
    where $\mathbf{y} = \alpha_t \operatorname{flip}(\epsilon) - \sigma_t \operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{z}_t)$ (assuming v-prediction).

This setup allows $f_{\theta'}$ to learn how to synthesize content in reverse while strictly following the motion trajectory dictated by the rotated attention maps from the forward pass.

### 3. Dual-Directional Diffusion Sampling
We will implement a joint sampling process (Algorithm 2) that fuses predictions from both directions to generate the final video $\mathbf{z}_0$.

Let $\mathbf{z}_t$ be the noisy video latent at timestep $t$. The process at each step $t$ from $T$ to $1$ is:

1.  **Forward Prediction:** Use the pre-trained model $f_\theta$ with start-frame conditioning $\mathbf{c}_0$:
    $$ \hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t,0} = f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t; t, \mathbf{c}_0) $$
    Simultaneously, extract the attention maps $\{A_i\}$.

2.  **Backward Prediction:**
    *   Flip the latent: $\mathbf{z}'_t = \operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{z}_t)$.
    *   Rotate the attention maps: $\{A'_i\} = \operatorname{rotate}(\{A_i\})$.
    *   Use the fine-tuned model $f_{\theta'}$ with end-frame conditioning $\mathbf{c}_{N-1}$:
        $$ \hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t,1} = f_{\theta'}(\mathbf{z}'_t; t, \mathbf{c}_{N-1}, \{A'_i\}) $$
    *   Flip the result back to the forward time-frame: $\hat{\mathbf{v}}'_{t,1} = \operatorname{flip}(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t,1})$.

3.  **Fusion and Update:**
    We fuse the predictions to ensure consistency. We will use a simple average, though we will also employ per-step recurrence (re-injecting noise and repeating the denoising step, e.g., 5 times) to enhance fusion stability:
    $$ \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t = \operatorname{fuse}(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t,0}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}'_{t,1}) $$
    $$ \mathbf{z}_{t-1} = \operatorname{update}(\mathbf{z}_t, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t; t) $$

The final video is obtained by decoding the clean latent $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_0)$.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework for Inbetweening:** We provide a methodology to adapt large-scale, single-image-conditioned video diffusion models for two-frame keyframe interpolation without massive resource expenditure.
2.  **Theoretical Motion Consistency:** By enforcing symmetry through rotated temporal attention maps, we theoretically ensure that the backward generation process mirrors the forward process. This eliminates the "back-and-forth" motion artifacts common in naive bi-directional sampling.
3.  **Parameter Efficiency:** We demonstrate that fine-tuning less than $2\%$ of the model parameters (specifically $W_v$ and $W_o$ in temporal layers) is sufficient to reverse the arrow of time in video generation, preserving the rich motion priors of the base model.

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
